t: Scientific Data Extractor: a plain-language overview
title: Scientific Data Extractor: a plain-language overview
description: Overview: what the Scientific Data Extractor does and why archives need it. A scientific data extractor reads research datasets and pulls out the numbers that matter: the measurements, their units, and what was being measured. It turns a messy spreadsheet or data file into clean, labeled values — temperature in degrees, distance in kilometers — ready for analysis and search.
provenance: Public methods compiled from standard information-extraction and knowledge-organization practice. Assembled for the JAH Databases archive.

t: How the Scientific Data Extractor works
title: How the Scientific Data Extractor works
description: Overview: what the Scientific Data Extractor does and why archives need it. Real extractors parse structured formats (CSV, NetCDF, HDF5) and semi-structured lab notebooks, using regular expressions to split values from units ('12.5 km', '3.2e-4 mol/L') and unit libraries like UDUNITS or Pint to normalize everything to standard units. Column headers and surrounding text are mined for variable names, instruments, and experimental conditions, and statistical profiling flags outliers and missing values. The output is a tidy variable table: name, value, unit, uncertainty, and provenance.
provenance: Public methods compiled from standard information-extraction and knowledge-organization practice. Assembled for the JAH Databases archive.

t: How the Scientific Data Extractor works: the deep tour
title: How the Scientific Data Extractor works: the deep tour
description: Overview: what the Scientific Data Extractor does and why archives need it. Real extractors parse structured formats (CSV, NetCDF, HDF5) and semi-structured lab notebooks, using regular expressions to split values from units ('12.5 km', '3.2e-4 mol/L') and unit libraries like UDUNITS or Pint to normalize everything to standard units. Column headers and surrounding text are mined for variable names, instruments, and experimental conditions, and statistical profiling flags outliers and missing values. The output is a tidy variable table: name, value, unit, uncertainty, and provenance. Advanced pipelines validate dimensional consistency (you cannot add meters to seconds), detect implicit units from instrument metadata, and align time series with different sampling rates through resampling. Quality is measured by value-level precision and recall against hand-curated datasets, plus unit-normalization accuracy. The hard cases are scanned tables requiring OCR, units hidden in footnotes, and legacy formats with undocumented encodings — those are quarantined with their raw bytes preserved rather than silently misread.
